title: AI Risk Management and Internal Controls

questions.question: What makes AI risk management actionable?
options: A broad governance principle stated without any supporting control evidence
A policy exception that gets approved quietly without visible review
An AI use case that moves to production without any named control owner
A named owner, a specific control, and evidence tied to that risk
questions.explanation: Governance becomes actionable with a named owner, a control, and evidence — not a principle with no evidence, a policy exception approved without review, or a use case with no owner at all.

questions.question: A team is granted a one-off exemption from the standard model-review process to hit a launch date, and the exemption is never logged or reviewed by anyone else. Which of the lesson's four signals does this match most directly?
options: Policy exception — a deviation from standard governance that hasn't gone through visible review
Control owner — no one is named as accountable for maintaining this control
Audit evidence — the records needed to prove a control ran are missing or incomplete
High impact — the use case affects a large number of people or a lot of money
questions.explanation: An unlogged, unreviewed exemption from standard review is the lesson's policy-exception signal — distinct from a missing control owner, missing audit evidence, or a use case simply being high impact.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A signed legal waiver that removes the need for further governance review
A ranked risk and control plan with governance next steps for each scenario
A complete, ready-to-file audit report covering the full use case
A neural network trained to automatically approve or reject risk exceptions unattended
questions.explanation: The artifact ranks scenarios into a risk-and-control plan with governance next steps — it doesn't issue a legal waiver, produce a finished audit report, or train a model to approve risks.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: Hiding control evidence so a later audit can't find gaps in the process
Skipping control tests because the use case seemed low risk at the time
Removing the approval owner once the risk register entry is closed
Audit trail — a record that lets someone later verify a control actually ran
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls are risk register, control test, audit trail, and approval owner — an audit trail lets someone verify later that a control ran, unlike hiding evidence, skipping tests, or removing the owner.

questions.question: When should an AI use case be escalated for governance review?
options: Only when there is no identifiable risk in the use case at all
Only after all control evidence has already been fully collected
When impact is high, control maturity is low, or a policy exception exists
Never — keeping a risk register is entirely optional for AI use cases
questions.explanation: High impact, weak control maturity, or a live policy exception are exactly when governance review should escalate — not the absence of risk, complete evidence, or treating the risk register as optional.

questions.question: What should be captured during delivery, not after launch?
options: Only informal chat comments exchanged during the sprint, with no record kept
Only a launch announcement sent to stakeholders once the feature is live
Control evidence and an audit trail that a reviewer can check later
No approvals, since the delivery team can self-certify the release
questions.explanation: Control evidence and an audit trail are easier and safer to capture during delivery than after launch — not informal comments, a launch announcement, or skipping approvals.
